Collapse several coders into one reference sheet

coder_reference.Rd

Takes the completed sheets and returns one sheet, so validate_sample(coder_reference(ana, luis, bea), res) composes without changing a signature. Read $ceiling from validate_sample() given the same sheets first. It says whether collapsing is honest, since a high alpha means the coders were interchangeable and a low one means the reference is a consensus that never existed.

Usage

coder_reference(
  ...,
  method = c("majority", "unanimous", "soft"),
  target = NULL
)

Arguments

...

Two or more completed coding sheets, as data frames or paths. Name them to name the coders.

method

A string naming how to collapse a row. "majority" takes the most common label, "unanimous" requires every coder to agree, "soft" keeps the disagreement as a proportion instead of resolving it. Default is "majority".

target

A string naming the label "soft" reports the proportion of. Defaults to the first of the two in sorted order, and the choice is written to the sheet so it is never implicit. Ignored by the other methods.

Value

A tibble, one row per document-item pair that any coder saw. It carries id, item, human_label, and n_coders and n_agree beside them.

Under "soft" the label column is replaced by human_prop, with human_target naming the label the proportion is of and n_target in place of n_agree. validate_sample() branches on which of the two arrived.

Collapse methods

"majority" writes the label most coders chose. Where two or more labels tie for the most it writes NA and names those rows, rather than breaking the tie. A rule that broke it would invent a coding no coder produced.

"unanimous" writes the label only where every coder who saw the row chose it, and NA otherwise. It warns, since the rows it discards are the hard ones, so what survives is easier than the draw was.

A row only one coder saw has a majority of one and is trivially unanimous. n_coders on the returned sheet is what separates those from a real agreement.

The soft method

"soft" writes no label. It writes human_prop, the share of coders who chose target, smoothed as (n_target + 1) / (n_coders + 2) so two coders who both said yes give 0.75 rather than 1. That is the honest reading of two observations, and it keeps the target off the boundaries, which matters because prob_renorm reaches exactly zero and a log score would then be infinite. validate_sample() scores it with Brier for the same reason.

It needs exactly two labels. Above two the honest soft target is a vector of proportions rather than one number, and reporting one label against the rest would leave a Brier over two categories where a label sheet is scored over all of them. Refused rather than silently rescaled.

See also

validate_sample(), whose $ceiling says whether collapsing is honest and which reads the result.

Examples

ana <- data.frame(
  id = c("1", "2", "3"), item = "q",
  human_label = c("YES", "NO", "YES")
)
luis <- data.frame(
  id = c("1", "2", "3"), item = "q",
  human_label = c("YES", "YES", "NO")
)
bea <- data.frame(
  id = c("1", "2", "3"), item = "q",
  human_label = c("YES", "NO", "NO")
)
coder_reference(ana = ana, luis = luis, bea = bea)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   id    item  human_label n_coders n_agree
#>   <chr> <chr> <chr>          <int>   <int>
#> 1 1     q     YES                3       3
#> 2 2     q     NO                 3       2
#> 3 3     q     NO                 3       2
